title: Errors Found by AI in the Research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
content:
Errors in the research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
138 papers audited
2,035 problems found
147 serious enough to change a headline number
69% of papers have at least one
97% of major and moderate errors with a clear direction overstate the paper’s claim
And on the method:
Two independent audits of each paper. One by Claude Opus 5.5, one by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, neither seeing the other’s work. Each obtained the paper, its appendices and its replication data, recomputed the headline numbers from the authors’ own files and, where possible, from the original sources (tax statistics, national accounts, Federal Reserve and survey data), checked that cited sources say what is claimed, and probed every assumption the conclusions rest on.
Then an adjudicator. A third agent re-verified every claimed problem, tried to refute each one, discarded those that did not survive, searched for problems both auditors missed, and graded what remained by how far it undermines the paper’s own headline claim: major changes a core number materially, moderate affects secondary results or a core result modestly, minor is a presentation or arithmetic slip. Confidence is graded separately.
There is much, much more at the link, which goes through the research paper by paper, and with further sustained analyses behind the links. The survey is both extensive and thorough. (And I thank an anonymous MR reader for this work.)
I am not even sure what to say at this point. We need a radical revaluation of this work, and of the associated policy arguments. More generally, this is only a single step in the story of how AI is going to revise economic science, and indeed past research more generally. As I stress in many of my recent talks, there will be significant gains and losses in status, with the losses often outweighing the gains. I see this as one of those cases.

report.summary: AI agents audited 138 papers by Saez and Zucman, finding 2,035 problems, many overstating headline claims and prompting calls for re-evaluation.
report.background: Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman are among the most influential economists studying inequality, taxation, and wealth distribution; their estimates have shaped policy debates over wealth taxes and tax enforcement. Their work relies on tax statistics, national accounts, survey data, replication files, and modeling assumptions, making it vulnerable to data and specification errors. The audit described here uses two independent AI agents, each given papers, appendices, and replication data, to recompute headline numbers and check cited sources, followed by a third adjudicator that tries to refute each finding and grades severity. This reflects a broader shift: AI is becoming a scalable layer for reproducibility checks in economics and beyond, raising questions about peer review, replication standards, and the reliability of research that underpins public policy.
key_points: The audit covered 138 papers and found 2,035 problems. Of those, 147 were serious enough to change a headline number, and 69% of papers had at least one issue. The scale suggests the findings are not isolated slips but a corpus-level reproducibility problem.

Direction mattered: 97% of major and moderate errors with a clear direction overstated the paper’s claim. That pattern is more troubling than random error because it suggests systematic bias in headline results rather than harmless noise.

The method was adversarial and independent. Two AI systems audited each paper without seeing each other’s work, recomputed numbers from authors’ own files and original sources, checked citations, and probed assumptions. A third agent then re-verified, tried to refute, discarded weak claims, and graded severity.

The article argues this demands a radical revaluation of the research and associated policy arguments. It also frames AI-driven auditing as a broader force that will revise economic science and past research, creating significant status gains and losses.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a showcase for agentic verification: long-horizon agents that read appendices, run replication code, cross-check citations, and adjudicate disputes. For developers, it signals demand for audit harnesses, provenance tracking, reproducible compute environments, and benchmarks that test whether agents can find real errors without hallucinating them. For regular users, the immediate impact is uncertainty: influential inequality and tax estimates may shift, and policy arguments built on headline numbers may need revision. The deeper effect is a change in trust infrastructure. AI can lower the cost of replication at scale, but it also concentrates power in whoever designs the auditors and adjudicators. The article’s warning about status losses is apt: many researchers and institutions may face reputational damage as past work is re-examined.
report.tools: Watch AI agent platforms from Anthropic and OpenAI for replication-style auditing, plus open-source reproducibility stacks such as R, Stata, Python, Docker, and Binder for rerunning authors’ code. Data-provenance tools like DVC and repository services such as Zenodo, Dataverse, and Code Ocean help preserve replication packages. Also follow agentic evaluation harnesses and open replication-checking projects that formalize independent audit, refutation, and severity grading.
